pages.n: How to read a candlestick chart
pages.s: On a candlestick chart, each candle shows a single period, such as one hour or one day. A candle carries four prices at once: the open, the high, the low and the close. The body spans the open and the close; the wicks show the extreme prices reached during that period.
t: Reading a candle step by step
k: Each candle shows one period; the length of that period is the timeframe.
The body spans the open and the close; the wicks show the extremes.
The colour tells you where the close sits relative to the candle's own open.
A single candle says little without its neighbours and the zones around it.

pages.s: A timeframe is the length of time a single candle covers on a chart: 15m is fifteen minutes, 1H one hour, 4H four hours, 1D one day and 1W one week. The same price move looks different on different timeframes, with a different number of candles and level of detail. Every reading makes sense only together with the timeframe it belongs to.
t: What each timeframe tends to be used for
When do candles open in crypto?
k: A timeframe is the length of time a single candle covers.
Several candles on a small timeframe are one candle on a larger one.
No timeframe is more correct than another; each describes a different span of time.
In crypto, candles open on UTC time on most exchanges.

pages.s: A candle is not final until its timeframe is over. Within the candle, price can move beyond a zone and then come back. At the close the candle's four prices are fixed. That is why whether a zone has broken, or whether a candlestick pattern has formed, is judged on the close.
t: Within the candle versus the close
Why the close is used as the measure
k: A candle is not final until its timeframe is over.
A move seen within the candle can be fully undone by the close.
Breakouts and patterns are judged on the closed candle.
When talking about a close, state the timeframe.

pages.s: Multi-timeframe analysis means looking at the same chart on more than one timeframe. The higher timeframe gives the context, meaning the main direction and the important zones; the lower timeframe shows in detail how price behaves within that context. A common sequence is to work top down, from 1D to 4H to 1H.
t: How timeframes can be read together
k: The higher timeframe is for context, the lower for detail.
A common sequence is 1D → 4H → 1H.
Three timeframes are often enough.
Each reading is written with the timeframe it belongs to.

pages.s: Price can be falling on the 1H chart while the rising structure holds on the 1D chart. This is not a contradiction but the same price read at two different scales. When each reading is stated with the timeframe it belongs to, both pictures can be true.
t: Stating a reading with its timeframe
k: Different timeframes describe different spans of time; both can be true.
A decline on a smaller timeframe can be a pullback on a larger one.
The larger structure is judged by its own timeframe's close and its last important low or high.
Stating each reading with its timeframe removes the apparent contradiction.

pages.s: A trend is price moving mostly in one direction over a period of time. It is read from the sequence of highs and lows: rising, falling or sideways. Identifying the trend is the first step to reading everything else on the chart in the right context.
t: How to read it on a chart
k: A trend is defined by the sequence of highs and lows.
A trend is always stated for a timeframe.
The last important low or high is the reference for when the structure breaks.
A trend describes the past; it does not guarantee it will continue.

pages.s: A swing high is a point where price stops rising and turns down, standing above the candles on either side. A swing low is the opposite. Trend, support and resistance all depend on marking these points correctly.
t: What are swing highs and lows?
k: A swing high is above the N candles on each side; a swing low is the opposite.
N is a choice; a small N picks more points, a large N fewer and more significant ones.
Not every candle's high is a swing high.
A swing high is confirmed once the candles to its right have closed.
Swing highs and lows depend on the timeframe.

pages.n: Higher highs, higher lows, lower highs, lower lows
pages.s: Each new swing high and low is labelled by comparing it with the previous one: higher high (HH), higher low (HL), lower high (LH) and lower low (LL). The sequence of these labels makes the direction of the trend measurable.
t: What do the four labels describe?
How the sequence defines the trend
k: Highs are compared with highs, lows with lows.
HH and HL describe a rising structure, LH and LL a falling one.
A trend is read from the sequence of labels, not from a single label.
Nearly equal highs or lows may sit inside the same zone.

pages.s: A BOS is when price closes beyond the last swing point in the direction of the trend. In an uptrend a close above the last swing high, in a downtrend a close below the last swing low, shows that the current structure continues. A wick is not enough; the close decides.
t: Three outcomes at the swing high
k: A BOS is a close beyond the last swing in the trend's direction.
A wick is not enough; the close must be clearly beyond the level.
A BOS signals continuation, not reversal.
Every BOS sets a new protected level.

pages.n: When does a trend count as changed?
pages.s: An uptrend counts as broken when price closes below the last important higher low. A first lower high can show the structure weakening; to speak of a new downtrend, a sequence of lower highs and lower lows is usually needed.
k: In an uptrend the reference is the last important higher low; in a downtrend, the last important lower high.
A first lower high shows weakening; on its own it does not change the trend.
The close, not the wick, breaks the structure.
A break is not the same as a confirmed new trend; confirmation needs an LH and LL sequence.

pages.s: A CHoCH is when the structure's protected level is broken by a close. In an uptrend a close below the protected low, in a downtrend a close above the protected high, shows that the structure has changed direction. Breaks of smaller lows and highs in between do not count as a CHoCH.
k: A CHoCH is a close beyond the protected level.
The first small break in the opposite direction is not a CHoCH.
A wick is not enough; the close must be beyond the level.
After a CHoCH the direction changes and a new protected level is set.

pages.s: A pullback is a temporary move against the trend that leaves the structure intact. In a reversal the structure breaks: the last important low or high is lost. The two look the same at first; where the move stops makes the difference.
k: A pullback keeps the structure; a reversal breaks it.
The reference point is the last important low or high.
Depth alone does not decide it.
For a reversal, the close and the next high or low matter, not the wick.

pages.s: A trendline is a sloping line drawn by joining the lows in an uptrend or the highs in a downtrend. Together with a parallel line through the opposite highs or lows, it forms a channel. It makes the trend's slope and pace visible, but drawing it is open to interpretation.
t: Is a trendline break a change of structure?
k: A trendline is drawn through at least two lows or highs; a third touch strengthens it.
A channel forms with a second line parallel to the trendline.
Choosing wicks or bodies changes the line; drawing it is subjective.
A break of the line is not the same as a break of structure.

pages.s: A range is price moving back and forth between two zones without a clear direction. Consolidation is the name often given to this pause, usually after a trend. A range ends with a close outside one of its edges and price staying there.
t: What usually happens inside a range
How it relates to the rectangle
k: In a range, highs and lows stay at roughly the same levels.
The edges of a range are zones, not lines.
Reactions come at the edges; indecision sits in the middle.
A range ends with a close outside an edge and price staying there.

pages.s: Support is a price area where falling price has stopped and turned up before; resistance is an area where rising price has stopped and turned down before. These areas come from past reactions. Because reactions happen over a range of prices rather than at a single one, they are better read as zones than as single lines.
t: Why a zone and not a line?
What makes a zone stand out
k: Support and resistance are areas where price has reacted in the past.
Reactions happen over a width, not at one price, so a zone is read as a band.
A zone is cleared by a close beyond its far edge.
A zone's past strength does not guarantee a future reaction.

pages.s: A level test is when price comes back to a support or resistance zone and reacts there. A test shows the zone is still being watched, but the close and the next candles decide the outcome. Whether repeated tests strengthen a zone or wear it down is read differently depending on the conditions.
t: Does each test strengthen or weaken a zone?
Signs of which reading fits better
k: A test is price arriving at a zone and reacting there.
The close and the next candles, not the wick, decide a test's outcome.
Repeated tests can confirm a zone or wear it down.
Look at how the reactions change, more than at how many tests there have been.

pages.s: A breakout is a candle closing beyond the far edge of a support or resistance zone. The close starts the breakout; the next candles staying beyond the zone strengthen it. Saying which timeframe's close you measure it on is part of the reading.
k: A breakout is measured by a close beyond the far edge.
A close inside the band is a test, not a breakout.
A single close is a start; follow-through shows in the next candles.
State which timeframe's close you measure the breakout on.

pages.n: False breakout: the wick versus the close
pages.s: A false breakout is when price moves beyond a support or resistance zone and returns behind it before the candle closes. On a chart it usually shows as a long wick. It is the close, not the wick, that decides a breakout.
t: Three outcomes at the same zone
k: The close, not the wick, decides a breakout.
The close should be beyond the zone's far edge; a close inside the zone is only a test.
A false breakout can show that the zone is still working.
A single wick is not enough; the next candles matter too.

pages.n: Sweep: a wick past the range edge
pages.s: A sweep is when price wicks beyond the top or bottom of a range and closes the candle back inside the range. Prices beyond the edge were not accepted in that candle. If the close stays outside the edge, the move is not a sweep but a breakout candidate.
t: Three outcomes at the range edge
k: A sweep is a wick past the range edge with a close back inside the range.
If the close stays outside the edge, it is a breakout candidate, not a sweep.
RH and RL are read as bands; a sweep is measured against the outer edge.
The chart shows that price could not stay beyond the edge, not that orders were there.

pages.n: Retests and role reversal: returning to a broken zone
pages.s: A retest is price returning to a zone after breaking it. On that return a broken resistance zone can act as support, and a broken support zone as resistance. This is called role reversal. Not every break gets a retest, and not every retest holds.
t: Not every break gets a retest
k: A retest is price returning to a zone it has broken.
Broken resistance can act as support, and broken support as resistance.
Closes, not wicks, decide how a retest turns out.
Not every break gets a retest, and not every retest holds.

pages.n: Historical highs and lows: references left by the past
pages.s: The all-time high (ATH), multi-year highs and lows, and the previous week's or month's high and low are reference areas anyone can see on a chart. Price often reacts as it nears them. Above an ATH, though, there is no level where price has traded before.
t: What are historical highs and lows?
Which levels count as historical references?
Why can behaviour change near an ATH?
Three pictures at an ATH zone
In crypto the data depends on the exchange
k: The ATH and multi-year and periodic highs and lows are reference areas everyone can see.
Above an ATH there is no old zone for price to react to.
An old high can act as support once it is broken.
Historical levels are read as zones, not lines.

pages.n: Psychological levels: why round numbers matter
pages.s: Psychological levels are round numbers such as 100,000 for BTC or 1.00 for some assets. Attention and orders can cluster around them, so price often reacts there. The reaction comes in a zone around the number, not at the exact number.
t: Why a zone and not an exact price?
k: Round numbers are levels where attention and orders can cluster.
The reaction comes in a zone around the number, not at the exact number.
Not every round number matters; scale and earlier zones decide.
A round number on its own is not proof of a turn or a breakout.

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of an uptrend and is made of three peaks. The middle peak (the head) is higher than the two on either side (the shoulders). It completes when price falls below the neckline that connects the two troughs, and it can signal that the uptrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bearish
Multi-candle
After an uptrend
Close below the neckline
Close above the right shoulder

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of a downtrend and is made of three troughs. The middle trough (the head) is lower than the two on either side (the shoulders). It completes when price rises above the neckline that connects the two peaks, and it can signal that the downtrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bullish
Multi-candle
After a downtrend
Close above the neckline
Close below the right shoulder

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of an uptrend, when price makes two peaks at roughly the same level. It completes when price falls below the neckline drawn through the trough between the peaks. It can signal that price failed to clear the same level twice and that the uptrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bearish
Multi-candle
After an uptrend
Close below the trough
Close above the second peak

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of a downtrend, when price makes two troughs at roughly the same level. It completes when price rises above the neckline drawn through the peak between the troughs. It can signal that price failed to break below the same level twice and that the downtrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bullish
Multi-candle
After a downtrend
Close above the peak
Close below the second trough

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of an uptrend, when price makes three peaks at roughly the same level. It completes when price falls below the neckline drawn through the two troughs between the peaks. It can signal that price failed to clear the same level three times and that the uptrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bearish
Multi-candle
After an uptrend
Close below the two troughs
Close above the third peak

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms at the end of a downtrend, when price makes three troughs at roughly the same level. It completes when price rises above the neckline drawn through the two peaks between the troughs. It can signal that price failed to break below the same level three times and that the downtrend is losing strength.
k: Reversal
Bullish
Multi-candle
After a downtrend
Close above the two peaks
Close below the third trough

pages.s: A triangle pattern formed by a flat resistance line and a series of rising lows. Price meets sellers at the same level each time, while buyers step in earlier on every pullback. It is most often read as a continuation pattern within an uptrend, and it completes with a close above the flat line.
k: Continuation
Bullish
Multi-candle
Within an uptrend
Close above the flat line
Close below the last low

pages.s: A triangle pattern formed by a flat support line and a series of falling highs. Price meets buyers at the same level each time, while sellers step in earlier on every bounce. It is most often read as a continuation pattern within a downtrend, and it completes with a close below the flat line.
k: Continuation
Bearish
Multi-candle
Within a downtrend
Close below the flat line
Close above the last high

pages.s: A triangle pattern formed by lower highs and higher lows converging on each other. Neither buyers nor sellers take control, and price is squeezed into a narrowing range. It is most often read as a continuation pattern because it tends to break in the direction of the prior trend, but it can break either way. The break decides the direction.
k: Continuation
Direction of the break
Multi-candle
Within a trend
Close outside one of the lines
Close outside the opposite line

pages.s: A pattern formed when price moves back and forth between two flat levels for a while. Sellers stop price at the upper level, buyers stop it at the lower level, and neither side takes control. It is most often read as a continuation pattern because it tends to break in the direction of the prior trend, but it can break either way. The break decides the direction.
k: Continuation
Direction of the break
Multi-candle
Within a trend
Close outside a boundary
Close beyond the opposite boundary

pages.s: A pattern in which both lines slope upwards and converge to the right. Price keeps making higher highs and higher lows, but the lower line is steeper than the upper one, so each new high clears the last by less. It is usually read as bearish, and it completes with a close below the lower line.
k: Reversal or continuation
Bearish
Multi-candle
After an uptrend or within a downtrend
Close below the lower line
Close above the last high

pages.s: A pattern in which both lines slope downwards and converge to the right. Price keeps making lower highs and lower lows, but the upper line is steeper than the lower one, so each new low undercuts the last by less. It is usually read as bullish, and it completes with a close above the upper line.
k: Reversal or continuation
Bullish
Multi-candle
After a downtrend or within an uptrend
Close above the upper line
Close below the last low

pages.s: A continuation pattern that forms when a sharp, fast move (the pole) is followed by a short pause in a narrow channel sloping against that move. It appears as a bull flag in a rise and a bear flag in a fall. It completes when the channel breaks in the direction of the pole, and it can suggest that the earlier move may carry on.
k: Continuation
With the trend
Multi-candle
After a sharp move (the pole)
Close outside the channel with the pole
Close beyond the flag's extreme

pages.s: A short pause that forms after a sharp, fast move (the pole) and is made of two small, converging lines. Price rests briefly, then most often breaks in the direction of the pole, which is why it is read as a continuation pattern. It can form in a rise or a fall; the pole and the break set the direction.
k: Continuation
Direction of the pole
Short (about 5–20 candles)
After a sharp move
Close in the pole's direction
Close outside the opposite line

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms after a decline, when a large green candle completely engulfs the body of the previous red candle. It can signal that selling pressure is fading and buyers are starting to take control.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Close below the low

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms after a rise, when a large red candle completely engulfs the body of the previous green candle. It can signal that buying pressure is fading and sellers are starting to take control.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Close above the high

pages.s: A two-candle reversal pattern that forms after a decline, when a green candle closes above the middle of the previous large red candle's body. It can show that more than half of the red candle's loss has been taken back and that buyers are starting to gain ground.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Close 2 above the midpoint of body 1
Close below the low

pages.s: A two-candle reversal pattern that forms after a rise, when a red candle closes below the middle of the previous large green candle's body. It can show that more than half of the green candle's gain has been given back and that sellers are starting to gain ground.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Close 2 below the midpoint of body 1
Close above the high

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms after a decline, when a large red candle is followed by a small green candle whose body sits entirely inside the red body. It can signal that selling pressure is pausing. It is considered a weaker signal than a bullish engulfing and usually waits for confirmation.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Body 2 inside body 1
Close below the low

pages.s: A reversal pattern that forms after a rise, when a large green candle is followed by a small red candle whose body sits entirely inside the green body. It can signal that buying pressure is pausing. It is considered a weaker signal than a bearish engulfing and usually waits for confirmation.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Body 2 inside body 1
Close above the high

pages.s: A single-candle reversal pattern that forms after a decline, with a small body and a long lower wick. It shows price falling sharply within the candle and recovering towards the close. It can suggest that sellers were unable to hold price lower.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Lower wick ≥ 2 × body
Close below the low

pages.s: A single-candle reversal pattern that forms after a rise, with a small body and a long lower wick. Its shape is the same as a hammer; the difference is the context. It can show price dropping clearly within the candle and the rise meeting serious selling for the first time.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Lower wick ≥ 2 × body
Close above the high

pages.s: A single-candle reversal pattern that forms after a decline, with a small body and a long upper wick. It shows buyers trying to lift price within the candle. Even though the attempt does not hold until the close, it can suggest that selling pressure is starting to ease.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Upper wick ≥ 2 × body
Close below the low

pages.s: A single-candle reversal pattern that forms after a rise, with a small body and a long upper wick. It shows price climbing clearly within the candle and falling back towards the close. It can suggest that the higher prices were not accepted.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Upper wick ≥ 2 × body
Close above the high

pages.s: A single-candle reversal pattern made of one long wick and a small body. The long wick points to the side where price was tried and pushed back. A pin bar with a long lower wick is called bullish, one with a long upper wick bearish. It can signal that the market has refused a price level.
k: Reversal
Either way
Wick ≥ 2/3 of range
At the end of a move
Close beyond the wick's tip

pages.s: A single candle whose open and close are almost the same, leaving a very small body. Price moved during the candle but returned to where it started by the close. It can show indecision: neither buyers nor sellers won over that period.
k: Indecision
Undecided
Body ≤ 10% of range
After a move or at a zone
Close outside its range

pages.s: A single candle with a small but visible body and wicks of similar length on both sides. Price moved both ways during the candle, but the close stayed near the open. It can show indecision: neither buyers nor sellers took control over that period.
k: Indecision
Undecided
Body ≈ 10–30% of range
After a move or at a zone
Close outside its range

pages.s: A three-candle reversal pattern that forms after a decline. A large red candle is followed by a small-bodied candle, and then by a green candle that closes past the middle of the first candle's body. It can signal that selling pressure has stalled and buyers are starting to step back in.
k: Reversal
Bullish
After a decline
Close above body 1's midpoint
Close below the low

pages.s: A three-candle reversal pattern that forms after a rise. A large green candle is followed by a small-bodied candle, and then by a red candle that closes below the middle of the first candle's body. It can signal that buying pressure has stalled and sellers are starting to step back in.
k: Reversal
Bearish
After a rise
Close below body 1's midpoint
Close above the high

pages.s: Volume is the amount traded during the period a candle covers. It is shown as a bar for each candle below the chart. Volume measures participation in the market; on its own it does not say which way price will go. In crypto, the volume of the same asset varies by exchange and data provider.
t: Why crypto volume looks different from place to place
The volume of an open candle
k: Volume is the amount traded during a candle.
The bar's colour shows the candle's direction, not buying or selling.
Crypto volume varies by exchange and data source; compare within one source.
Spot and derivatives volume measure different markets.
Volume describes participation; on its own it does not give direction.

pages.s: Reading price and volume together shows how much participation came with a move. Volume rising or falling along with the move can lead to different readings. These readings are hints; on their own they do not say what price will do next.
t: What price and volume show together
How to read it on a chart
Time of day and day of week in crypto
k: Price shows direction, volume shows participation; read them together.
Judge volume against earlier candles, not by its absolute size.
A rise on rising volume can read as acceptance, on falling volume as fading strength; neither is certain.
A hint from volume is confirmed by price closes and structure.

pages.s: When judging a breakout, the breakout candle's volume is compared with the average volume of recent candles. Volume clearly above that average shows high participation in the move beyond the zone. The close still decides the breakout; volume is information that goes alongside it.
t: Why look at volume on a breakout?
k: The close decides the breakout; volume is information that goes alongside it.
The breakout candle's volume is often compared with the average of the last 20 candles.
There is no universal threshold for clearly high volume.
High volume does not prove a breakout will hold, nor low volume that it will fail.

pages.s: A volume profile spreads the volume traded over a chosen period by price instead of by time. It is drawn as horizontal bars beside the chart. The price with the most trading is the POC, and the range holding most of the volume is the value area (between VAH and VAL).
t: How to read it on a chart
k: A volume profile shows volume by price, not by time.
The POC is the most traded price; the value area is the range holding usually 70% of the volume.
Thick nodes are ranges where price stayed, thin nodes ranges it moved through quickly.
The profile changes with the chosen period and data source.

pages.n: What is volatility? Contracting and expanding ranges
pages.s: Volatility is the size of price changes; it describes how much price moves, not which way. Markets swing between calm and active periods: ranges contract, then expand. The same percentage move can be unusual in a calm market and ordinary in a volatile one.
t: The same move, a different meaning
k: Volatility is the size of price changes; it does not describe direction.
Markets swing between periods of contraction and expansion.
The same percentage move means different things depending on the market's usual volatility.
Volatility measures describe the past; they do not say which way the next move goes.

pages.s: A price gap is when a candle opens above or below the previous candle's range without overlapping it, leaving an area of price where no trading took place. Gaps are rare on crypto spot charts, which trade 24/7. They are most often seen on CME Bitcoin futures, which close at weekends, and on low-liquidity pairs.
t: Why gaps are rare on crypto spot charts
Gaps on low-liquidity pairs and exchanges
k: A gap is an untraded area of price where the ranges of two candles do not overlap.
Real gaps are rare on crypto spot charts, which trade 24/7.
CME gaps come from the hours the futures market is closed; they do not show on the spot chart.
A gap filling is a possibility, not a rule, and when it fills is unknown.

pages.s: An FVG is the gap left between the wicks of the candles on either side of a strong candle. In that range price traded only in one direction, and quickly. Later candles can come back into the gap and fill it partly or completely.
k: An FVG is the gap between the wicks on either side of a strong candle.
A bullish FVG fills from above, a bearish FVG from below.
If a close goes beyond the far end of the gap, the FVG is invalidated.
There is no guarantee that an FVG will fill or act as support or resistance.

pages.s: After a large move in a short time, price can follow one of three broad paths: it can continue in the same direction, move sideways, or give back part of the move. Which one it will be is often not clear from the first candles. After sharp moves, volatility tends to stay high for a while.
t: Why the first reaction can mislead
k: After a sharp move, continuation, consolidation and partial retracement are three possible pictures.
Volatility clusters; large candles tend to be followed by large candles.
The first reaction does not on its own show what follows; closes and zones make it clearer.
Zones passed through quickly are tested for the first time if price comes back.

pages.n: What are indicators, and what are their limits?
pages.s: A technical indicator is a line or value calculated from price and volume data with a formula. It summarises information that is already on the chart in a different form; it adds no new information and usually lags price. Knowing which question it answers and where it can mislead is the first step to reading it well.
t: Several indicators are not several pieces of evidence
k: Indicators are calculated from price and volume; they summarise rather than add information.
Most indicators lag price.
Trend, momentum, volatility and volume indicators answer different questions.
Settings change the result; defaults are not correct values.
Agreement between indicators built from the same data is not independent evidence.

pages.s: A moving average is the average of the closing prices of the last given number of candles, recalculated with every new candle. The simple average (SMA) gives every close equal weight; the exponential average (EMA) gives recent closes more weight. Both smooth price, and both lag behind it.
t: Which question does a moving average answer?
k: The SMA weights the last N closes equally; the EMA gives recent closes more weight.
The EMA multiplier is 2 ÷ (N + 1).
Every moving average trails price; the longer the period, the larger the lag.
20, 50 and 200 are common choices, not rules.
Crossovers describe a change of direction; they do not announce its outcome.

pages.s: RSI is a momentum indicator that shows, on a scale of 0 to 100, how strong recent up closes have been compared with down closes. The default setting is 14 periods. The 70 and 30 lines are widely used, but a reading above 70 does not mean price "must fall", nor one below 30 that it "must rise".
k: RSI is the ratio of 14-candle gains to losses, smoothed with Wilder's method.
The scale is 0–100; 50 marks balance.
Above 70 does not mean price must fall, nor below 30 that it must rise.
In strong trends RSI can stay in the extreme areas for a long time.

pages.s: MACD is the difference between the 12- and 26-period exponential moving averages. A 9-period average of that difference forms the signal line, and the gap between the two forms the histogram. It shows how far the short-term average is from the long-term one, and whether that distance is growing or shrinking.
k: MACD = EMA 12 − EMA 26; the signal line is the 9-period EMA of MACD.
The histogram is the difference between MACD and the signal line.
MACD crossing zero is the two averages crossing.
Crossovers trail price and can be frequent and misleading in sideways markets.

pages.s: Bollinger Bands are two bands drawn two standard deviations either side of a 20-period simple moving average. The bands narrow when price calms down and widen when it becomes active, so they show volatility on the price chart. Price touching a band is not a signal on its own.
t: Which question do Bollinger Bands answer?
What does a band touch tell you?
k: Default setting: 20 SMA ± 2 standard deviations.
The bands narrow as volatility falls and widen as it rises.
In a strong trend price can walk along a band; a touch is not a signal on its own.
A squeeze can point to an expansion, but not to its direction.

pages.s: ATR is the average of the candles' true range; it shows how much price typically moves in one candle, in price units. The default setting is 14 periods with Wilder smoothing. ATR measures the size of moves, not their direction.
t: What it is commonly used for
k: The true range is the largest of high − low and the two distances from the previous close.
Default setting: 14 periods with Wilder smoothing.
ATR measures the size of moves, not their direction.
To compare different price levels, ATR is divided by price.

pages.s: VWAP is the volume-weighted average of the prices traded since a chosen starting point. Prices that traded on heavy volume affect the average more. Crypto has no sessions, so VWAP is anchored to a point: usually the start of the UTC day, the week, or a chosen event.
k: VWAP = cumulative (typical price × volume) ÷ cumulative volume.
Crypto has no sessions; VWAP is anchored to the UTC day, the week or a chosen event.
VWAP is often read as the period's fair-value reference, but it does not guarantee a reaction.
The result depends on the exchange's volume.

pages.s: An AVWAP is the volume-weighted average of the prices traded since a chosen point, such as an important high or low. Whether price is above or below it shows where price stands against the average price of those who traded since that point.
t: Three states between price and the AVWAP
k: An AVWAP is the volume-weighted average price since a chosen point.
When the anchor changes, the AVWAP changes.
Price holding above it means those who bought since that point are on average in profit.
There is no guarantee that an AVWAP acts as support or resistance.

pages.s: OBV is an indicator that accumulates volume by the direction of the close: a candle's volume is added when the close rises and subtracted when it falls. The question it asks is whether volume is building up on the same side as price. What matters is the slope of OBV, not its absolute value.
t: In crypto, volume depends on the exchange
k: OBV adds volume on a higher close and subtracts it on a lower close.
Read the slope and the highs and lows, not the absolute value.
Moving with price reads as confirmation; parting from it reads as divergence.
In crypto, volume depends on the exchange; say which data you use.

pages.s: ADX is an indicator that measures the strength of a trend, not its direction. Two more lines that carry the direction are drawn with it: +DI and −DI. The question it asks is whether price is moving clearly in one direction or going back and forth in a directionless range.
k: ADX measures a trend's strength, not its direction.
+DI and −DI show the direction; the default setting is 14.
Below about 20 reads as weak, above 25 as trending; these are conventions.
ADX lags; a falling ADX means fading strength, not a reversal.

pages.s: Divergence is when the highs and lows of price and of an oscillator (such as RSI, MACD or OBV) point in different directions. For example, price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high. It can suggest that a move is losing momentum, but it says nothing about when, or even whether, price will turn.
t: How to read it on a chart
Why it is not a timing signal
k: Divergence is the indicator not confirming price's extreme.
Regular divergence can suggest fading momentum, hidden divergence a continuing trend.
In strong trends, divergence can form again and again and come to nothing.
It is not a timing signal; at a zone it offers more meaningful context.

pages.n: How to read an economic calendar
pages.s: An economic calendar shows the time and importance of upcoming data releases and decisions, with their previous, expected and actual values, in a single table. What markets react to is often not the figure itself but how far the actual value differs from the forecast. In crypto, which trades 24/7, that reaction shows on the chart the moment the figure is released.
t: The crypto chart at the moment of release
k: Markets often react not to the figure but to how far it differs from the forecast.
A revision to the previous figure can change how a release reads.
US data mostly come at 08:30 ET, which is 12:30 or 13:30 UTC depending on daylight saving.
Looking at the candle close rather than the wicks at the release is a calmer measure.

pages.s: Markets react to events not only when they happen but from the moment they are expected. An outcome that is widely expected may already be reflected in price before the event; at the event, the move is often decided by the unexpected part. That is why an expected rate cut may not lift prices.
t: Why an expected rate cut may not lift prices
k: Price reflects what is known and expected in advance.
At the event, the reaction is often decided by the unexpected part.
An expected rate cut may not lift prices if the guidance is tighter than expected.
How much is priced in cannot be measured directly, only estimated.

pages.s: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets the US Federal Reserve's policy rate at eight scheduled meetings a year. The decision is released at 14:00 ET and a press conference follows at 14:30 ET. Markets compare not only the decision but also the statement, the projections and hints about next steps with expectations.
t: What is the FOMC and what does it decide?
How the market's expectation is followed
What to look at on decision day
k: The FOMC sets the target range for the federal funds rate at eight scheduled meetings a year.
The decision comes at 14:00 ET and the press conference at 14:30 ET; 18:00 or 19:00 UTC depending on daylight saving.
The dot plot is published at the March, June, September and December meetings; minutes follow three weeks later.
The reaction is often decided by how far the decision differs from expectations and earlier guidance.

pages.s: In the US, inflation is followed every month through two main releases: the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the BLS and the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index from the BEA. The Fed's inflation goal is defined in terms of PCE. Markets compare the headline and core figures, and the monthly and yearly changes, with expectations.
k: The BLS publishes CPI and the BEA publishes the PCE price index each month; both mostly come at 08:30 ET.
Core figures leave out food and energy; markets often look at core more closely.
The Fed's 2 per cent goal is defined in terms of PCE.
The monthly change shows the recent trend, the yearly change the last twelve months; base effects can move the yearly figure.

pages.s: US jobs data shows how strong the labour market is. The most watched release is the monthly nonfarm payrolls report; weekly jobless claims give a more frequent reading in between. Markets usually read these figures through their likely effect on the Fed's rate decisions.
t: What is the nonfarm payrolls report?
The main figures in the report
Why the data is read through Fed expectations
Crypto trades 24/7, the data comes at a set time
k: The nonfarm payrolls report usually comes on the first Friday of the month at 08:30 ET.
Jobless claims are published every Thursday at 08:30 ET.
Markets compare the figure with the forecast; revisions shape the reaction too.
Strong data is often read as a tighter Fed outlook, but that is not a rule.

pages.s: Growth data shows how fast the US economy is expanding or slowing. GDP gives a broad, backward-looking measure every quarter; PMI surveys and retail sales give earlier signals each month. Markets read these figures through growth and rate expectations.
k: GDP is released quarterly as an annualised quarter-on-quarter growth rate.
GDP comes in three stages: advance, second and third estimates.
On a PMI, above 50 points to expansion and below 50 to contraction.
Markets compare the figure with the forecast; the same data can be read differently in a different context.

pages.n: Bond yields and the yield curve
pages.s: The yield on US Treasuries sums up the market's rate, growth and inflation expectations in a single number. Plotting the yields of different maturities side by side gives the yield curve. Yields can affect many markets, crypto included, through the dollar and risk appetite.
t: How yields can affect risk assets
k: A bond's price and its yield move in opposite directions.
The 2-year yield is more sensitive to Fed expectations, the 10-year to long-term expectations.
An inverted yield curve is a warning sign, not a timing tool.
Why yields move can change how they affect risk assets.

pages.s: The dollar index (DXY) measures the US dollar against six major currencies in a single number. The euro makes up more than half of the basket. It is often said to move against crypto and gold, but that link is not constant.
t: The inverse link with crypto and gold
k: DXY measures the dollar against a basket of six currencies.
About 57.6% of the basket is the euro; the index largely moves with EUR/USD.
Rate differentials and risk appetite are the main drivers of DXY.
The inverse link with crypto and gold is a tendency, not a fixed rule.

pages.s: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are indices that sum up the overall direction of the US stock market, and they are widely used to read the market's risk appetite. Crypto sometimes moves together with them, especially around the US session open and close. The relationship changes over time and is not one of cause and effect.
t: What do stock indices tell you?
k: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are broad gauges of risk appetite in the US stock market.
In crypto, volume and volatility often pick up around the US session open and close.
The correlation between crypto and the indices changes over time.
Moving together is not cause and effect; there may be a common driver.

pages.n: Crypto-specific events: token unlocks, halvings, ETF flows
pages.s: Token unlocks, the Bitcoin halving, spot ETF flows and network upgrades are events specific to the crypto market. Most have dates known in advance, so the expected effect may already be priced in before the event. How an event will show up in price is always uncertain.
k: Most crypto-specific events have dates known in advance.
The size of an unlock is judged relative to circulating supply.
A halving cuts the rate of new Bitcoin supply in half roughly every four years.
The effect of a known event may already be priced in; the reaction on the day is uncertain.

pages.s: The gold/silver ratio shows how many ounces of silver one ounce of gold can buy. It sums up in one number how expensive or cheap the two metals are relative to each other. The ratio has moved within a very wide range over the decades, and reaching an extreme does not mean it will come back.
k: Ratio = price of one ounce of gold ÷ price of one ounce of silver.
The ratio measures the two metals' relative performance, not direction.
Silver's industrial demand, higher volatility and smaller market move the ratio.
The ratio has ranged very widely over the decades; there is no fixed "normal" level.
An extreme reading does not guarantee a return to the mean.

pages.s: Gold pays no interest or dividend. So the cost of holding it depends on the return available elsewhere, especially the real rate of interest after inflation. Gold often tends to move against real rates and the dollar, but that relationship has clearly weakened in some periods.
t: Why is gold sensitive to real rates?
Different pictures from the same data
k: Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation expectations; the most watched measure is the 10-year TIPS yield.
Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost changes with real rates.
Gold often tends to move against real rates and the dollar.
The relationship has weakened in some periods, for example during strong central-bank buying.

pages.n: Gold and silver on crypto exchanges
pages.s: On crypto exchanges gold and silver can trade in two ways: tokens backed by physical gold, and perpetual futures that track the gold or silver price. These products trade 24/7, while the traditional market is closed at weekends. That difference changes how weekend prices and Monday opens should be read.
k: On crypto exchanges gold and silver trade through tokens and perpetual futures.
The traditional market is open nearly 24 hours on weekdays but closed at weekends.
The weekend price can drift on thin liquidity and jump at the open.
A token depends on its issuer; a perpetual on the exchange's index and funding rate.
